title: Liability law for touching someone else's debris
bottleneck: Under the 1972 Liability Convention and the Outer Space Treaty, a launched object remains the property and responsibility of its launching state forever — there is no salvage law in orbit. Removing another nation's dead satellite without permission is legally ambiguous at best and could be construed as an attack on a space asset; a debris-removal arm is also an anti-satellite weapon. No international framework authorizes third-party removal, so every mission needs bespoke bilateral permission.
why_it_blocks: The highest-risk objects are often foreign military or defunct state assets; without legal clarity, removers can only touch their own countries' junk — a fraction of the problem.
current_state: No binding international removal regime exists; interagency guidelines are voluntary. ClearSpace-1 targets ESA's own hardware precisely to sidestep the issue.
